sections.text: About I build Android apps at ████████, focused on community features — plus the unglamorous work that decides whether an app feels fast: a customizable payment library on Google Play Billing, a resource controller that made dynamic lists behave, liveness, and macro-benchmarking of UI-layer resource use. I measure before I believe. When an existing tool could not answer a question, I wrote the harness: an inspector for WebSocket traffic, and a benchmark for how coding agents decide what to read. Both started as side projects and ended up changing how I work. This site is built the same way. Each project is an exploded view of how it is actually put together — layer by layer, component by component, with the numbers that came out of the measurements. Measuring what an AI reads before it codes.

I build Android apps at ████████, focused on community features — plus the unglamorous work that decides whether an app feels fast: a customizable payment library on Google Play Billing, a resource controller that made dynamic lists behave, liveness, and macro-benchmarking of UI-layer resource use.

I measure before I believe. When an existing tool could not answer a question, I wrote the harness: an inspector for WebSocket traffic, and a benchmark for how coding agents decide what to read. Both started as side projects and ended up changing how I work.
This site is built the same way. Each project is an exploded view of how it is actually put together — layer by layer, component by component, with the numbers that came out of the measurements.

I build Android apps at ████████, focused on community features — plus the unglamorous work that decides whether an app feels fast: a customizable payment library on Google Play Billing, a resource controller that made dynamic lists behave, liveness, and macro-benchmarking of UI-layer resource use.

This site is built the same way. Each project is an exploded view of how it is actually put together — layer by layer, component by component, with the numbers that came out of the measurements.

Every WebSocket frame, captured and inspectable.

A drop-in Scarlet WebSocket decorator for Android: it records every frame into Room and exposes sessions in a Compose inspector launched from a persistent notification. Built as a reusable library with a deliberately thin sample host.
Solo Android engineer — library design, Compose UI, Room persistence, benchmark integration
An inspector for the invisible half of Android networking.

WebSocket traffic is the hardest part of an Android app to debug: frames fly past, sessions blend together, and logcat gives you a wall of text with no notion of a session. Existing HTTP inspectors stop at request/response — they do not understand long-lived sockets.

Mirror the decorator idea onto Scarlet: a WebSocketFactory wrapper and a WebSocket decorator record each frame into Room, tag it with a session identity resolved by a tracker, and surface the result through a foreground-service notification that opens a Compose UI. The library keeps a four-file public surface so internals stay free to change, and skips DI frameworks entirely — constructor parameters instead.

The sample host runs two Scarlet clients against one endpoint and the inspector captures both into separate sessions, with frames replayable in a list → detail flow from the notification. The app then became the benchmark target for my JEV decision-hook research — fifteen refactor tasks across ten rule areas.

Measuring what an AI reads before it codes.

A zero-dependency Node harness that runs the same fifteen refactor tasks against a real Android codebase under three context strategies, scores what each one chose to read, and checks every claim it makes against the repository instead of trusting it.
Solo engineer — harness, adapters, fixtures, scoring, analysis
How much of a repo does a model need to read before it decides where to look?

Coding agents burn context on orientation. The expensive question is not what a piece of code does — it is which six files matter for this task. Agents answer that by reading far more than they need, and nobody measures whether the skipping was right.

A zero-dependency Node harness runs fifteen refactor tasks against a real Android codebase under three arms: full context, the JEV decision model (a third-party service I do not own), and a native baseline. Each arm's section selection is scored against hand-labelled gold sections, the code it produces is compiled, and every claim about tests is checked against the repository rather than trusted.

Selective context cut median input tokens by 25% and cost by 17%, and every arm compiled on all 45 runs — but it lost recall against gold sections (0.79 vs 1.00). The honest result is a trade-off curve, not a victory, which is exactly what a benchmark is for.
Runs one arm over one task set.
Entry point: parses the arm, the target and the repeat count, resets the target repository to its baseline tag, then hands control to the runner.
Turns raw runs into a readable table.
Reads the per-run artefacts and prints the median/p90 table by arm — tokens, cache, cost, duration, recall.
Compares each run's selected sections with the hand-labelled gold set and reports precision/recall per task and arm.
Writes a target's hooks and rules.
Installs the hook settings and the per-arm CLAUDE.md variant into a target repository, so an arm is a configuration rather than a fork.

Checks what a subagent claims it did.
Pre-hook snapshots the tree; post-hook compares each claim — tests run, tests passing, build — against the actual repository state.
Classifies narration comments (what changed, why this way) versus contract comments, and blocks the former before they land.
Routes a task to a cheap or an expensive model by its shape; measured for tier choice, exploration need and change requests.
The only code that talks to the model.
One typed call to the decision model.
HTTP client with schema validation, timeouts and a replay mode so a run can be re-scored without spending tokens.
Keeps the state inside a hard ceiling.
Counts and trims the decision state to the configured budget before each call — the mechanism that makes 25% fewer tokens possible.
Refuses to read outside the target.
Validates every path against the allowed roots so a benchmark run can never wander into the rest of the machine.
Writes the run down as it happens.
Appends each request, decision and response to a run log that the report and the accuracy pass both read.
One task, one arm, one clean tree.
Drives the agent CLI, captures usage, enforces the turn cap and records incomplete runs rather than dropping them.
Task ids, prompts, expected areas and gold sections — the same fifteen tasks for every arm, so arms differ only in strategy.
Asserts the target is a git repo under an allowed root, resets it to the baseline tag and produces the diff stat after each run.
Per-model input, output, cache-read and cache-write rates, applied to every priced run so cost is comparable across arms.
Scores claims by model, not by vibes.
A structured judge that classifies claims and comments against a rubric; its agreement with human labels is reported, not assumed.
Frozen request/response cases so the scoring code can be tested and re-run without touching a live model.
The sections a human says each task actually needs — the standard every arm is scored against, including the arm that loses.
Where a run becomes a number.
Per-run JSON plus the median/p90 tables by arm; the raw material for every figure this project claims.
A single measured run: reset the target, ask the model what to read, let the agent work, record everything.
After the runs: compare what each arm read against the answer key, then price and publish.
